tldr: WeaveRL integrates GPU-parallel 3D surfel reconstruction directly into the loop of massively parallel reinforcement learning (RL) across thousands of environments, feeding sensor-derived dynamic geometric maps into a collision-avoidant controller (Geometric Fabrics) to learn from scratch and transfer to real hardware policies that safely operate in collision-dense environments.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of WeaveRL. Batches of depth images from parallel simulation environments are fused at high speed into a surfel map and passed directly to Geometric Fabrics to compute obstacle repulsive forces. The policy leaves collision avoidance to the fabric and focuses entirely on generating target commands to accomplish the task.
overview:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved impressive success in acquiring dexterous robot skills, but manipulation in geometrically complex, obstacle-dense scenes remains difficult. Prior approaches have largely fallen into two camps: end-to-end methods that learn motor commands directly from images or point clouds, or structured control methods that supply hand-specified geometric primitives (such as spheres and cuboids) to safety controllers like Geometric Fabrics. The former struggles because geometric reasoning and control are entangled in a single network, while the latter suffers from an inability to adapt to complex real-world shapes and scene changes.

To address this dilemma, the authors asked: what if we rapidly reconstruct a 3D geometric map from sensor observations during RL rollouts and pass it directly to the safety controller? To realize this, they developed a surfel-based (small circular disk patches) 3D reconstruction pipeline that packs thousands of simulation environments into contiguous GPU tensors for batched processing. By instantly computing collision repulsive forces from this dynamic geometry and feeding them into Geometric Fabrics, the RL policy is freed from worrying about collision avoidance and can concentrate solely on task completion.

For validation, the authors constructed four manipulation tasks with tight geometric constraints in Isaac Lab Arena, including cluttered tabletop picking, boxing, and shelf insertion. While baselines relying on hand-specified primitives or point cloud observations failed to learn on complex tasks, WeaveRL was the only method that stably acquired policies across all tasks. Furthermore, when tested with novel, unseen obstacles not present during training, WeaveRL significantly improved collision-free task completion from 35% to 61% and transferred zero-shot to a physical Franka arm.
contributions: Proposed a high-throughput 3D surfel reconstruction pipeline that batches thousands of parallel simulation environments as GPU tensors without bottlenecking RL rollout speeds.
Built the first learning framework to integrate the exact same real-time 3D reconstruction in-the-loop across all stages of massively parallel RL: training, distillation, and real-robot deployment.
Extended the inputs to Geometric Fabrics from hand-specified primitives to sensor-derived dynamic surfel maps, enabling robust collision avoidance in complex scenes.
Demonstrated high avoidance performance against unseen test-time obstacles without policy retraining, as well as zero-shot sim-to-real transfer to a physical manipulator.

sections.heading: Capturing complex environments: The dilemma between end-to-end and structured control
sections.summary: Robots operating in the real world require accurate geometric scene perception, but constructing an efficient environment representation inside RL has been an open problem. End-to-end learning entangles perception, geometry, and control, whereas structured control has been constrained by static, hand-specified primitives. This paper resolves this trade-off by coupling GPU-parallel 3D reconstruction directly into the RL loop.
sections.details:
Deploying robots to unstructured environments like factories and homes requires them to accurately perceive and act upon scene geometry. While reinforcement learning (RL) has enjoyed immense success in quadruped locomotion and manipulation, avoiding complex obstacles using camera sensors remains a steep challenge.

The dominant approach today is end-to-end visuomotor policies that take camera images or point clouds as input and directly output low-level control commands. While flexible, this requires a single neural network to handle visual perception, geometric reasoning, and motor control simultaneously, drastically increasing sample complexity.

Another promising route is structured control, where a high-level learned policy sits on top of a control-theoretic collision-avoidance controller (such as Geometric Fabrics). Traditionally, however, obstacles have had to be manually specified by humans as simple geometric primitives (spheres, cuboids) or provided as static pre-scanned maps. This fails when faced with shifting real-world environments or intricate, irregular geometries.

This is the breakthrough: if we can construct accurate 3D geometric maps from sensor inputs in real time across thousands of parallel RL environments and pipe them directly into Geometric Fabrics, we can get the best of both worlds. The authors developed a GPU-optimized batched 3D reconstruction method and introduced WeaveRL, bridging perception and control without sacrificing computational throughput.

sections.heading: Context in related work: Batched reconstruction, structured control, and reactive policies
sections.summary: Existing 3D mapping libraries are designed for single-instance real-world deployment and cannot run inside parallel RL training loops. Similarly, prior structured control and reactive neural policies have failed to seamlessly marry sensor-driven dynamic maps with massively parallel RL. WeaveRL stands out by linking batched surfel reconstruction directly to Geometric Fabrics for learning policies from scratch.
sections.details:
### Batched 3D Reconstruction for RL
Building world models from raw sensor data at the scale required by RL has long been a computational bottleneck. Policies operating on point clouds can react to the current geometry, but they have no memory of occluded regions. Meanwhile, high-fidelity mapping libraries using surfels, signed distance fields (SDFs), or occupancy grids are engineered for single-robot real-world deployments; they cannot be embedded into training loops that run thousands of simulation environments simultaneously. WeaveRL adopts a batched architecture across thousands of environments, enabling online 3D reconstruction in-the-loop for the first time.

### Environment Representations for Structured Control
Geometric controllers like Geometric Fabrics and RMPflow provide powerful frameworks for stabilizing robot motion by geometrically structuring a safe action space. However, prior works (e.g., DextrAH) largely rely on hand-specified geometric primitives. While some studies connect sensor-derived SDFs or point clouds to fabrics, they only use hand-crafted target attractors and do not learn task-level policies via RL.

### Reactive Neural Motion Policies
End-to-end methods generating trajectories directly from sensors (such as Flow Motion Policy or Deep Reactive Policy) exist, but sampling-based collision checks cannot theoretically guarantee zero collisions and typically require pre-training on tens of millions of expert steps. In contrast, WeaveRL maintains Geometric Fabrics throughout training, allowing policies to be trained from scratch without expert demonstrations.

sections.heading: A unified architecture fusing parallel surfel reconstruction and Geometric Fabrics
sections.summary: A differentiable surfel reconstruction pipeline processes thousands of environments on a single GPU using fixed-size tensors and boolean masks. Analytical, closed-form Euclidean distances and gradients to robot collision spheres are rapidly computed from the surfels and supplied as repulsive accelerations to Geometric Fabrics, allowing the policy to focus solely on task objectives.
sections.details:
### III-A Batched 3D Reconstruction for Parallel Environments
To represent environment geometry, the method uses a collection of surfels $\mathcal{S}_t = \{\mathbf{s}_i\}$—small circular disks defined by position $\mathbf{p}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, normal $\mathbf{n}_i \in \mathbb{S}^2$, and radius $r_i$. To handle $N_b$ parallel RL environments efficiently without variable-length per-environment lists, the entire state is allocated on GPU memory as a fixed-shape tensor $[N_b, C, F]$, where $C$ is maximum surfel capacity and $F$ is feature dimensionality.

Active surfels are tracked via a boolean mask matrix $\mathbf{B} \in \{0, 1\}^{N_b \times C}$ and packed into indices $[0, N_{\mathrm{valid}})$. As new RGB-D frames arrive, backprojection, data association, and surfel integration/addition are executed via vectorized GPU kernels across the batch dimension. Because it is implemented within a standard deep learning framework, the entire pipeline is differentiable, allowing potential backpropagation into visual encoders in the future.

### III-B Scene-Aware Fabrics for Dense Collision Manipulation
Geometric Fabrics are second-order reactive controllers that combine multiple independent motion behaviors into a stable dynamical system. Given the robot configuration coordinates $q$, the fabric requires the local Euclidean distance field $\Phi_t(\mathbf{x})$ and its spatial gradient $\nabla\Phi_t(\mathbf{x})$ to perform obstacle avoidance.

The robot arm is approximated by multiple collision spheres (centers $\mathbf{x}_k(q)$, radii $\rho_k$) placed along the kinematic chain. The distance $d_i(\mathbf{x})$ from any query point $\mathbf{x}$ to a surfel disk and the direction (gradient) to its closest point have analytical closed-form solutions. The global distance field is computed with minimal overhead as the minimum over all surfels: $\Phi_t(\mathbf{x}) = \min_i d_i(\mathbf{x})$.

For each collision sphere $k$, the obstacle clearance $d_k = \Phi_t(\mathbf{x}_k) - \rho_k$ and outward unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_k = \nabla\Phi_t(\mathbf{x}_k)$ are computed. When clearance drops below a threshold $d_{\max}$, a repulsive acceleration $\ddot{\mathbf{x}}_k^{\mathrm{rep}} = \frac{k_r}{d_k^2} \hat{\mathbf{u}}_k$ activates. Geometric Fabrics combine policy-specified attractor accelerations with these sensor-derived repulsive accelerations to solve for safe joint accelerations $\ddot{q}$. Because the fabric handles all low-level collision avoidance, the RL agent can focus entirely on reaching task-oriented goals.

sections.heading: Experimental findings: Massive throughput, clearing geometric tasks, and robustness to novel obstacles
sections.summary: The proposed batched surfel reconstruction achieved up to 12.1x throughput over a standard baseline (nvblox) across 1024 parallel environments. Furthermore, it was the only method to master all four complex manipulation tasks, such as boxing and narrow shelf insertion. It delivered over 1.7x higher collision-free success (61%) under unseen obstacles compared to baselines and transferred zero-shot to a physical Franka arm.
sections.details:
### IV-A Benchmarking Batched 3D Reconstruction
Using a tabletop manipulation dataset, the authors compared their method against nvblox (sequential per-environment looping) on a single NVIDIA L40 GPU across 1 to 1024 parallel environments. Beyond 32 environments, the proposed method surpassed nvblox, achieving a 12.1x speedup at 1024 environments against nvblox (1cm voxel size) and 3.3x against the 5cm setting, while keeping GPU memory to a modest 10.6 GB. Reconstruction accuracy (at a 3cm threshold) reached 99.8%, proving it generates high-fidelity geometry at extraordinary throughput.

### IV-B Manipulation Under Geometric Constraints
Four tasks were evaluated on a Franka arm: simple pick, cluttered tabletop pick, box pick-and-place, and shelf insertion. An asymmetric teacher policy with privileged information was trained and distilled via DAgger into a student policy taking stereo RGB images. Automatic Domain Randomization (ADR) dynamically adjusted task difficulty up to a maximum level (ADR=50).

- Teacher Training Success: Baselines using hand-specified primitives or direct point-cloud encoders failed to reach ADR=50 on geometrically constrained tasks like boxing and shelf insertion. Only the proposed Surfel fabric consistently completed training across all tasks over 5 random seeds.
- Robustness to Novel Obstacles: Policies trained on tabletop picking were evaluated with an unseen cylindrical obstacle added at test time. Hand-specified primitive baselines dropped to 35% collision-free success and point cloud policies to 6%, while WeaveRL maintained 61% success (a 1.7x to 10x improvement). The student policy also preserved an edge (36% vs. 21%).
- Real Robot Deployment: All four tasks were successfully deployed on a physical Franka arm. In the shelf task, the robot inserted cubes accurately without colliding with the narrow opening.
- Occlusion Robustness: Comparing the proposed temporal surfel accumulation against single-frame reconstruction revealed that even when the arm itself occluded obstacles, WeaveRL retained past geometric memories and safely avoided collisions.

sections.heading: Conclusions and horizons: Overcoming static camera limits toward full end-to-end learning
sections.summary: WeaveRL unlocks manipulation in geometrically dense scenes by weaving real-time 3D reconstruction and structured controllers inside massively parallel RL. Future directions include addressing persistent blind spots caused by static cameras via wrist-mounted cameras and exploiting differentiability for joint visual representation learning.
sections.details:
This work establishes WeaveRL, a groundbreaking framework that fuses sensor-driven, real-time 3D reconstruction into Geometric Fabrics while maintaining the massive throughput of parallel RL. By moving away from hand-crafted primitives and offloading collision avoidance to dynamic geometric maps built from raw sensor data, WeaveRL solves complex geometric tasks where prior baselines failed, exhibits high robustness to novel obstacles, and enables smooth sim-to-real transfer.

Key limitations noted in the paper include:
- Reliance on workspace-fixed static cameras, which can leave persistent occlusions unreconstructed. Extending the setup to dynamic viewpoints, such as head- or wrist-mounted cameras, is a natural next step.
- Although the tensorized reconstruction pipeline is fully differentiable, gradients were not backpropagated through it in these experiments. Jointly optimizing upstream visual encoders and mapping end-to-end represents an exciting future direction.

sections.heading: Appendix: Tabletop reconstruction dataset and computational breakdown
sections.summary: Details are provided for the tabletop reconstruction dataset created in Isaac Lab Arena and released with the paper, along with a profiling breakdown of step times and memory during RL training. Teacher step times are split evenly between rendering, mapping, and mask operations, pointing to clear optimization paths.
sections.details:
### A-A Tabletop Manipulation Reconstruction Dataset
The benchmark dataset was generated using Isaac Lab Arena. It consists of 10 trajectories of 500 frames each (5000 frames total at $1200 \times 680$ resolution) recorded by an orbiting camera around a fixed table and Franka arm. Scenes feature clutter items like bins, bowls, and mugs, and include ground-truth camera trajectories and cropped ground-truth meshes.

### Computation Time and Memory Breakdown
For teacher training running 1024 environments on a single GPU, the step time was 385 ms. This is roughly equally split across rendering (98 ms), surfel mapping (93 ms), and image mask processing to exclude the arm and grasped object (90 ms). GPU memory consumed 23.5 GB (9.5 GB for fabrics, 7.6 GB for rendering, 6.5 GB for surfel processing), with host RAM reaching 88 GB due to rendering overhead. While 8 NVIDIA L40 GPUs were used to run 8192 environments, total training steps matched primitive-based baselines (~8000 rollouts, ~37–39 hours of wall-clock time), suggesting training times will drop significantly as parallel rendering and mapping pipelines are further optimized.

takeaways: In structured control approaches separating geometric safety from task-level RL, dynamically supplying environment geometry from GPU-parallel surfel reconstruction—rather than fixed primitives—is remarkably effective.
To maintain rollout throughput in parallel RL, abandoning per-environment variable lists and compiling all environments into a unified tensor-and-mask layout is essential.

Placing an explicit geometric reconstruction layer into the controller eliminates the need for the RL policy to learn obstacle avoidance from scratch under sparse rewards, automatically providing strong generalization and collision avoidance against unseen obstacles.
limitations: Relying on static camera placements leaves persistent blind spots unmapped, creating potential collision risks in occluded areas.
Additional overhead from depth rendering and 3D mapping increases hardware requirements (from 1 GPU to 8 GPUs) and wall-clock training time compared to primitive-based approaches.

In tight spaces with dense, tiny obstacles, current fabric repulsive parameter tuning can cause overly conservative avoidance behavior, slightly lowering task completion rates in specific configurations.
